newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: New Colombia envoy could smooth relations with U.S..
newsitem.headline: New Colombia envoy could smooth relations with U.S..

text.p: Colombia's rocky relationship with the United States took a turn for the better on Thursday when President Ernesto Samper named Defence Minister Juan Carlos Esguerra to fill the post of ambassador to Washington.

Former attorney Esguerra, 47, said he would work to normalise ties between Bogota and Washington, which became strained this year amid the scandal sparked by allegations that Samper funded his 1994 election campaign with drug money.

"There have been a series of difficulties in our relations with the United States and there are many challenges ahead. One of the main challenges will be to take relations back to the point where they were before," said Esguerra in a news conference just after his appointment.

Esguerra, a Cornell University graduate, has taken a lead role in the fight against drug trafficking and the counter- insurgency campaign against Colombia's leftist guerrillas during his two years at the Defence Ministry -- a background likely to please the Clinton administration.

The top diplomatic post has been vacant since April, when Carlos Lleras de la Fuente quit, blaming his resignation on accusations of Samper's close ties with drug kingpins, particularly billionaire chieftains of the Cali drug cartel.
Lleras' departure followed the United States' decision to decertify Colombia as an ally in the war against drugs.

Three months later, the United States further humiliated Colombia by withdrawing Samper's U.S. entry visa, citing his "known" links to drug lords, even though he had been cleared of any wrongdoing in an inquiry by the Colombian Congress.
"Rewinning certification is obviously a prime goal. I will also be looking to get the Colombian government's voice heard in Washington," Esguerra said.

Samper announced the appointment at an event to sanction a tough law, passed by Congress last week, designed to strip drug barons of their ill-gotten gains. Esguerra will take up his post early January. His successor has not been named.

The Colombian government hopes that law will help pacify Washington and at the very least spare the country from the threat of U.S. economic sanctions in retaliation for its perceived failure to crack down enough on drug trafficking.
Political analysts, however, agree Esguerra will have to work hard to convince the Clinton administration to recertify Colombia in March 1997.

Washington praised the asset forfeiture law but has made no secret of its wish to see Bogota lift its constitutional ban on the extradition of Colombians to the United States and for stiffer sentences to be introduced for convicted drug traffickers in Colombia.
